name: Multidirectional shoulder instability
populations: people with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder
summary: Symptomatic shoulder instability in more than one direction, usually atraumatic and often with generalised laxity. Rehabilitation is the first treatment but its evidence is limited; surgery is for failures.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Supervised rehabilitation over 12 weeks to 6 months: in a randomised trial the Watson program beat the Rockwood program at 12 and 24 weeks (12 weekly sessions plus home exercise)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No MDI-specific return-to-sport criteria were found; use criteria on strength, scapular control and absence of apprehension

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Sulcus sign with Beighton score, apprehension and load-and-shift; sulcus sign and load-and-shift had only moderate intertester reliability (kappa 0.39–0.73 across six tests)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Clinical diagnosis. MRI or MR arthrography for labral tears or to exclude other pathology; imaging does not diagnose MDI

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Teens and young adults: median age 24.3 years (range 9–56) across 861 shoulders in a systematic review

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No reliable incidence found. After physiotherapy, 21% (52 of 253) needed surgery in a systematic review

overview:
Multidirectional instability (MDI) is symptomatic subluxation or dislocation of the glenohumeral joint in at least two directions, often in young, active people [r1]. It can arise from underlying atraumatic laxity, repetitive microtrauma or a traumatic injury, and often occurs with generalised ligamentous laxity or an underlying connective tissue disorder [r2]. The static and dynamic stabilisers become incompetent through congenital or acquired causes, and it is critical to distinguish laxity (a physical finding) from instability (symptoms), and MDI from unidirectional instability with generalised laxity [r3,r2].

Rehabilitation is the recommended first treatment, but the evidence is thin. A Cochrane review found no completed randomised trial comparing exercise with placebo, no treatment or usual care, so its benefit and harm are uncertain [r1]. A systematic review of exercise versus surgery found only 4 non-randomised studies, all at high risk of bias, with very low-quality evidence [r4]. The best trial compared two programs: in 41 people with non-traumatic MDI, 12 weekly sessions of the Watson program produced better WOSI, MISS and pain outcomes than the Rockwood program at 24 weeks [r5]. An older uncontrolled series found good or excellent results in 80% of 66 shoulders with atraumatic subluxation but only 16% of 74 with traumatic subluxation [r6].

When well-delivered rehabilitation fails, open inferior capsular shift or arthroscopic capsular plication are used. In a systematic review of 24 articles (861 shoulders), 21% of those treated with physiotherapy needed surgery, and redislocation after surgery occurred in 7.5% after open capsular shift and 7.8% after arthroscopic plication, versus 24.5% after thermal shrinkage and 22% after laser-assisted capsulorrhaphy [r7]. Outcomes remain inferior to those of traumatic unidirectional instability [r3], and evidence for the best post-operative rehabilitation is lacking [r8].

epidemiology.text: Reliable population incidence figures for MDI were not found in the sources reviewed. It affects young, active people [r1]. In a systematic review of 24 articles (861 shoulders in 790 patients), the median age was 24.3 years (range 9–56), the dominant side was involved in 58% of shoulders, and median follow-up was 4.2 years [r7]. In a single-group rehabilitation study of 43 people with MDI, the mean age was 19.8 years and 27 were female [r9]. Generalised hypermobility is common in the population and depends on the Beighton cut-off: in 778 school-aged children the prevalence was 19.2% at a Beighton score of 4 or more, 9.5% at 5 or more and 5.7% at 6 or more [r10], so a hypermobility label alone does not make a shoulder unstable. Of 253 patients treated with physiotherapy in the systematic review, 52 (21%) needed surgery [r7].

intrinsic: Generalised ligamentous laxity or an underlying connective tissue disorder [r2]
Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder: MDI was the problem treated in a randomised trial of 21 such patients [r11]
Altered scapular kinematics: decreased scapular lateral (upward) rotation, increased scapular internal rotation and antero-inferior decentring of the humeral head [r12]
Abnormally functioning dynamic stabilisers (poor muscle control), which is why motor-control retraining is the focus of rehabilitation [r2]
Younger age (teens and twenties) and female predominance in rehabilitation cohorts (27 of 43 in one) [r9], although sex differences in incidence were not established
extrinsic: Repetitive microtrauma from overhead and throwing sports and swimming [r2]
A traumatic episode in an already lax shoulder [r2]
Repeated end-range loading, such as gymnastics, dance or deliberate end-range stretching (clinical convention)

mechanism.summary: MDI usually has no single injury moment. A lax capsule and incompetent dynamic stabilisers, from congenital or acquired causes [r3], allow the humeral head to translate under little load: downward when carrying, forward in overhead or throwing positions, and backward when pushing or pressing. Scapular positioning is often altered, with reduced scapular lateral rotation, increased internal rotation and antero-inferior decentring of the head [r12]. Repeated end-range loading, or one minor event in an already lax shoulder, then produces pain, apprehension and subluxation or dislocation in more than one direction [r2].
sequence: The glenohumeral capsule and ligaments are lax, from congenital connective tissue differences or repeated stretching, so the joint volume is increased [r3,r2].
A load or movement pushes the head toward the limit of the lax restraints, for example a downward pull when carrying a bag, or the cocked overhead position.
The dynamic stabilisers (rotator cuff and scapular muscles) must centre the head, but their control is often poor: the scapula rotates less and the head sits antero-inferiorly [r12].
With inadequate muscular control, the head translates inferiorly, anteriorly or posteriorly, causing pain, a sense of slipping or subluxation.
Repeated episodes stretch the capsule further and the person guards, which can worsen motor control and loss of confidence (a proposed cycle, not directly measured).
Symptoms spread across several directions and everyday activities, and the shoulder may sublux or dislocate with minimal force [r1].

variants.name: Atraumatic MDI with generalised laxity
variants.description: Gradual onset in a young person with generalised ligamentous laxity and a positive sulcus sign. The commonest form treated in rehabilitation trials [r5,r9].

variants.name: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder
variants.description: MDI in people with a connective tissue disorder. In a randomised trial of 21 such people, both home-based programs improved WOSI by 240 points at 12 weeks and 325 at 24 weeks, with no difference between programs and no non-exercise control group [r11].

variants.name: Repetitive microtrauma in athletes
variants.description: Repeated overhead loading in swimmers, throwers and gymnasts can stretch the capsule and produce symptoms in several directions [r2].

variants.name: Post-traumatic MDI
variants.description: A traumatic episode in a lax shoulder. Traumatic subluxation did far worse with an exercise program (16% good or excellent) than atraumatic subluxation (80%) in an older series [r6].

variants.name: Voluntary or positional instability
variants.description: Some people can displace the shoulder on demand. This needs a different, behavioural and motor-control approach, and the sources reviewed here do not address it.

anatomy.text: The glenohumeral joint relies on static and dynamic stabilisers. Static stabilisers are the capsule and glenohumeral ligaments, the labrum, and the shape of the bone; the rotator interval capsule resists inferior translation. Dynamic stabilisers are the rotator cuff, the long head of biceps and the scapular muscles, which centre the head in the glenoid and position the socket. Instability occurs when static and dynamic stabilisers become incompetent from congenital or acquired causes [r3]. In MDI the capsule is lax and the joint volume increased, and scapular kinematics are altered [r12].

structures.name: Glenohumeral capsule and ligaments
structures.role: Static restraint at end range; lax or redundant in MDI [r3]

structures.name: Rotator interval capsule and coracohumeral ligament
structures.role: Resists inferior translation; the role of rotator interval plication is controversial in surgery [r3]

structures.name: Glenoid labrum
structures.role: Deepens the socket and anchors the capsule; tears can coexist

structures.name: Rotator cuff
structures.role: Dynamic stabiliser that compresses and centres the head; poor control is typical

structures.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
structures.role: Position the glenoid; scapular lateral rotation is reduced in MDI [r12]

structures.name: Long head of biceps
structures.role: Contributes to anterosuperior stability in elevated positions

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
MDI can arise from underlying atraumatic laxity, repetitive microtrauma or a traumatic injury, and often occurs with generalised ligamentous laxity or connective tissue disorders [r2]. The core problem is incompetence of the static and dynamic stabilisers [r3]. A non-systematic review of scapular kinematics found that people with multidirectional glenohumeral instability had antero-inferior decentring of the humeral head, decreased scapular lateral rotation and increased scapular internal rotation [r12].

Laxity is not instability: increased translation on examination is common and may be asymptomatic, while instability is symptomatic [r3]. A hypermobility label depends on the cut-off used, and prevalence changes severalfold between Beighton thresholds [r10]. Structural lesions such as labral tears can coexist, but MDI is mainly a problem of capsular volume and motor control.

structures.name: Glenohumeral capsule and ligaments
structures.effect: Lax and redundant, so the head translates further than normal, often in inferior and one or more other directions [r3,r2]

structures.name: Rotator interval
structures.effect: Laxity contributes to inferior and anterior translation; plication is sometimes added in surgery, though its role is controversial [r3]

structures.name: Labrum
structures.effect: May tear or be normal; not the primary lesion in atraumatic MDI

structures.name: Scapulothoracic motion
structures.effect: Reduced scapular lateral rotation and increased internal rotation, with antero-inferior head decentring [r12]

muscles.name: Rotator cuff
muscles.effect: Poor co-contraction and endurance to centre the head; 'abnormally functioning' dynamic stabilisers are a treatment target [r2]

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
muscles.effect: Altered activation with reduced scapular lateral rotation; rehabilitation after a postural strategy builds these muscles first [r12]

muscles.name: Deltoid and large movers
muscles.effect: Tend to dominate over the cuff, so the head is poorly centred during elevation (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Trunk and hip muscles
muscles.effect: Contribute to the load transmitted through the arm, especially in sport; addressed in kinetic-chain work

cellular.description: Repeated end-range loading elongates capsular collagen and increases laxity; there is often no discrete injury and little inflammation.
A symptomatic episode brings synovitis and capsular irritation that settle with relative rest.

cellular.phase: Surgical healing (if capsular shift or plication)
cellular.description: Fibroblasts lay down new collagen that tightens the capsule, then remodelling aligns the fibres over months; the optimal post-operative rehabilitation is not established [r8].

systems.effect: Altered neuromuscular control of the scapula and humeral head is typical, with dynamic stabilisers that function abnormally [r2]; motor-control retraining is therefore central.

Kinesiophobia and fear of movement are common; in a randomised trial in hypermobile patients, kinesiophobia scores did not change significantly with a home exercise program, and the authors suggested a supervised multidisciplinary approach might help [r11].
Generalised ligamentous laxity or a connective tissue disorder (for example hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) is often present [r2,r11].
Scapular kinematics, thoracic posture and trunk control change shoulder loading; rehabilitation addresses posture and the whole shoulder complex [r12].
Synovitis and capsular irritation accompany symptomatic episodes and settle with load management.

timeframes.summary: Rehabilitation trials delivered 12 weekly physiotherapy sessions with a home program and measured outcomes at 6, 12 and 24 weeks [r5], or a 6-month home-based program [r11]. After surgery, the optimal rehabilitation is not established [r8].

healing.description: Explain the condition, correct posture and scapular position, activate the cuff and serratus anterior in mid-range.
Train cuff co-contraction and scapular upward rotation through the working range, with low-load, high-repetition work.
Progress resistance, closed-chain loading, and overhead and sport-specific positions; outcomes were measured at 24 weeks in the main trial [r5].
Graded return to sport and a long-term maintenance program; a surgical opinion is considered if an adherent, supervised program fails.

milestones.label: Complete 12 weekly sessions of the supervised program
milestones.note: As in the Watson versus Rockwood trial [r5]

milestones.label: First outcome review of function and scapular control
24-week outcome point
milestones.note: Between-program differences were largest at 24 weeks [r5]

milestones.label: Review need for surgery after an adequate, adherent program

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. No MDI-specific return-to-sport criteria were identified in the sources reviewed. Use symptom control, strength, scapular control, kinetic-chain function and psychological readiness, with a graded return to the provocative positions (clinical convention).

symptoms: Nonspecific activity-related shoulder pain and decreased athletic performance are common presenting complaints [r3]
A feeling of the shoulder slipping, 'giving way' or going out in more than one direction, often with minimal force
Pain or a sense of slipping with carrying (inferior), overhead reaching (anterior) or pushing (posterior)
Symptoms in both shoulders and in other joints (hypermobility)
Fear of moving the shoulder into end-range positions
signs: A visible sulcus below the acromion with downward traction on the arm
Generalised ligamentous laxity (Beighton score; cut-offs vary)
Excess translation in more than one direction, often with a normal-looking resting shoulder
Scapular dyskinesis: reduced scapular lateral rotation on elevation [r12]
Apprehension or reproduction of symptoms in several positions

subjective: Onset: atraumatic or a minor event, and number of episodes of subluxation or dislocation
Provoking positions and directions: carrying (inferior), overhead (anterior), pushing (posterior)
Bilateral symptoms, other joints, and family history of hypermobility or connective tissue disorders
Sport, training load and recent changes; pain pattern and night symptoms
Voluntary component, fear of movement and psychological stress
Previous treatment and adherence, and goals (return to sport, work, avoiding surgery)
observation: Sulcus at rest or with downward traction
Scapular position and dyskinesis during elevation and lowering
Posture: forward head, thoracic kyphosis and protracted shoulders
General signs of hypermobility: skin, scars and joint hyperextension
palpation: Posterior cuff and scapular muscle tone and tenderness
Joint line and bicipital groove for coexisting pathology
AC joint and clavicle to exclude other pain sources
rangeOfMotion: Excess passive external rotation at the side compared with the other side, and generalised hypermobility
Beighton score: prevalence changes severalfold with the cut-off (19.2% at 4 or more versus 5.7% at 6 or more in children), so interpret with age, sex and symptoms [r10]
Elevation and horizontal adduction with scapular palpation or observation
Do not stretch the lax shoulder into end range as part of assessment beyond what is needed
strength: Rotator cuff strength and endurance, comparing sides with a hand-held dynamometer
Scapular strength and endurance (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
Scapular upward rotation during elevation, as measured in trials [r9]
neuro: Cervical screen to exclude cervical radiculopathy as the source of arm symptoms
Neurological screen of the upper limb if there are traction symptoms with carrying
Vascular check if arm positions provoke neurovascular symptoms (consider thoracic outlet syndrome)
functional: Overhead reach, hand behind head and hand behind back
Closed-chain stability: wall push-up plus and quadruped weight shifts
Sport-specific tasks: swimming stroke, throwing, gymnastic support positions
Kinetic-chain screen: single-leg balance, trunk rotation and hip control

specialTests.name: Sulcus sign
specialTests.procedure: With the arm at the side and relaxed, apply downward traction at the elbow or wrist and look for a sulcus below the acromion. Repeat in external rotation.
specialTests.positive: A visible sulcus below the acromion that does not reduce in external rotation suggests rotator interval and inferior laxity. In a reliability study of 40 people, the sulcus sign had moderate intertester reliability and needed further standardisation, and the validity of the instability and laxity tests has not been studied [r13]. No accuracy figures are quoted.

specialTests.name: Load-and-shift test
specialTests.procedure: Seated or supine, stabilise the scapula, apply an axial load to centre the head, then translate the head anteriorly and posteriorly and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Increased translation compared with the other side, with or without symptoms. Intertester reliability was moderate in one study of 40 people [r13]. Increased translation alone is laxity; reproduction of the person's symptoms indicates instability [r3].

specialTests.name: Apprehension and relocation tests
specialTests.procedure: Supine, arm abducted to 90° and externally rotated; relocation applies a posterior force on the proximal humerus.
specialTests.positive: Apprehension or pain relieved by the relocation force. Apprehension showed substantial intertester reliability and relocation only fair reliability in the same study [r13]. No accuracy figures for MDI are quoted.

specialTests.name: Gagey hyperabduction test
specialTests.procedure: With the scapula stabilised, passively abduct the arm in the frontal plane and measure the angle reached, comparing sides.
specialTests.positive: Greater abduction than the other side suggests inferior glenohumeral ligament laxity. Intertester reliability was substantial in one study [r13]. No accuracy figures are quoted.

specialTests.name: Beighton score
specialTests.procedure: Nine-point score (thumb to forearm, little finger extension, elbow and knee hyperextension, and forward flexion with palms to the floor).
specialTests.positive: Positive cut-offs vary with age and sex, and prevalence depends strongly on the threshold chosen [r10]. A high score supports a generalised laxity phenotype but does not diagnose shoulder instability.

clinicalRules.name: Distinguish laxity from instability
clinicalRules.description: Increased translation is a finding; instability is symptomatic translation. It is critical to distinguish increased laxity from instability, and MDI from unidirectional instability with generalised laxity, to maximise treatment success [r3,r2].

clinicalRules.name: Diagnosis rests on history and examination, and clinicians differ
clinicalRules.description: In a survey of 888 clinicians, orthopaedic surgeons weighted examination findings and physiotherapists and athletic trainers weighted history, and they differed in their diagnoses of an athlete with instability and impingement signs [r14]. Agree on explicit criteria (symptoms, direction, laxity, motor control) rather than relying on one test.

outcomeMeasures.name: Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index (WOSI)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the Watson versus Rockwood trial and the hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos trial [r5,r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Melbourne Instability Shoulder Score (MISS)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the Watson versus Rockwood trial [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Oxford Shoulder Instability Score
outcomeMeasures.use: Instability-specific outcome used in a single-group rehabilitation study [r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: DASH, Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia and Global Rating of Change
outcomeMeasures.use: Secondary outcomes in the hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos trial [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Scapular upward rotation and hand-held dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Secondary measures of scapular position and strength in rehabilitation studies [r9]

imaging.indication: Not routinely needed; use if trauma, locked dislocation or bone abnormality is suspected
imaging.findings: Excludes fracture, glenoid dysplasia or osteoarthritis

imaging.indication: Persistent pain, suspected labral tear, or surgical planning; not to diagnose MDI
imaging.findings: Labral tears, capsular volume and rotator interval; imaging findings must match the symptoms and examination

imaging.indication: Suspected cuff tear or when dynamic assessment is helpful
imaging.findings: Cuff pathology and, in some settings, dynamic translation

differentials.name: Anterior shoulder dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: A traumatic event, unidirectional anterior instability and a Bankart lesion, without generalised laxity or a sulcus sign.

differentials.name: Posterior shoulder instability
differentials.distinguishing: Symptoms in a flexed, adducted and internally rotated arm, with a positive jerk or Kim test, and no inferior or anterior component.

differentials.name: SLAP lesion
differentials.distinguishing: Overhead pain with mechanical symptoms and biceps-labrum provocation; may coexist with MDI.

differentials.name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain
differentials.distinguishing: Painful arc and pain on resisted movement, without apprehension or a sense of slipping.

differentials.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Neurovascular symptoms (paraesthesia, heaviness) with arm positions rather than a sense of the shoulder slipping.

differentials.name: Long thoracic nerve palsy (scapular winging)
differentials.distinguishing: Painless scapular winging with weak serratus anterior and difficulty elevating, without laxity.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Neck-origin symptoms with dermatomal findings and reproduction with Spurling or neck movement.

redFlags: An acute traumatic dislocation that does not reduce, or a pale, cold or pulseless hand: emergency department. Document the axillary nerve and distal pulses before and after reduction.
A fixed, internally rotated arm after a seizure or electric shock: posterior dislocation. Image and refer urgently; do not force external rotation.
New neurological deficit (weakness, numbness or reflex change), or symptoms spreading beyond the shoulder: consider cervical or brachial plexus pathology and refer.

Features of a heritable connective tissue disorder with systemic involvement (for example arterial or organ problems, or a strong family history): medical review, because the shoulder may be one expression of a broader condition (clinical convention).
Constant night or rest pain, fever or weight loss: consider infection or tumour and refer for imaging.
Marked distress, self-harm or a prominent voluntary component: involve a psychologist or doctor, and avoid surgery until addressed.
After surgery: fever, wound drainage or severe escalating pain suggest infection; refer back to the surgeon the same day.

management.principles: Start with a clear explanation and a supervised, specific exercise program focused on scapular and rotator cuff motor control, followed by strength and function. Rehabilitation is the recommended initial treatment, but the evidence is weak: a Cochrane review found no completed trial of exercise versus no treatment [r1], the one randomised comparison of two programs favoured the Watson program over the Rockwood program [r5], and exercise versus surgery evidence is very low quality [r4]. Reserve surgery (open inferior capsular shift or arthroscopic capsular plication) for people whose symptoms persist after an adequate, adherent program [r3,r2]. Avoid thermal or laser capsular shrinkage [r7], and set expectations, because outcomes after surgery remain inferior to traumatic unidirectional instability [r3].

medical.name: Analgesia and activity modification
medical.description: Short-term analgesia and temporary reduction of provocative end-range loading to settle symptoms while rehabilitation starts. No specific trials were found.

medical.name: Arthroscopic capsular plication or open inferior capsular shift after failed rehabilitation
medical.description: In a systematic review of 24 articles (861 shoulders), 21% (52 of 253) of those treated with physiotherapy needed surgery. Redislocation occurred in 7.5% (17 of 226) after open capsular shift and 7.8% (21 of 268) after arthroscopic plication; the authors concluded that both are the best surgical procedures after failed rehabilitation, with arthroscopic plication comparable to open shift [r7]. Outcomes remain inferior to those of traumatic unidirectional instability [r3]. The review is a level IV systematic review of level I to IV studies, so the evidence is low-level.

medical.name: Rotator interval plication as an adjunct
medical.description: The role of rotator interval capsular plication is controversial, though it may augment plication in patients with specific patterns of instability [r3].

medical.name: Thermal capsular shrinkage or laser-assisted capsulorrhaphy
medical.description: Redislocation occurred in 24.5% (12 of 49) after arthroscopic thermal shrinkage and 22% (11 of 55) after arthroscopic laser-assisted capsulorrhaphy, much higher than after plication or open shift [r7].

medical.name: Surgery as first-line treatment
medical.description: Most people respond to or can manage with rehabilitation: 79% (201 of 253) of those treated with physiotherapy in the systematic review did not need surgery [r7], and 80% of 66 shoulders with atraumatic subluxation had good or excellent results with an exercise program in an older series [r6]. Exercise is the recommended first treatment [r3,r2]. Early surgery in atraumatic MDI exposes people to surgical risks for a condition that often responds to rehabilitation.

physio.name: Supervised, specific exercise program (for example the Watson MDI program)
physio.description: In a randomised trial of 41 people with non-traumatic, non-structural MDI, 12 weekly physiotherapy sessions with a home program of the Watson MDI program were more effective than the Rockwood program: WOSI effect size 11.1 (95% CI 1.9–20.2) at 12 weeks, and at 24 weeks WOSI 12.6 (95% CI 3.4–21.9), MISS 15.4 (95% CI 5.9–24.8) and pain −2.0 [r5]. In an uncontrolled study of 43 people, a 12-week program improved functional scores (WOSI SMD −3.04), scapular upward rotation in 0–60° of abduction, and strength [r9]. There is no randomised trial of exercise against no treatment or usual care [r1], and exercise-versus-surgery evidence is very low quality (surgery better on impairment measures, exercise on patient-reported measures) [r4].

physio.name: Home-based exercise therapy in hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder
physio.description: In a randomised trial of 21 patients with MDI, two 6-month home-based programs both improved WOSI (240 points at 12 weeks and 325 at 24 weeks), DASH (8.6 points at 24 weeks) and global rating of change, with no difference between programs; kinesiophobia did not change significantly, and the authors suggest supervised multidisciplinary care may be more effective [r11]. There was no non-exercise control group, so improvement cannot be attributed to exercise alone.

physio.name: Scapular and postural motor-control retraining
physio.description: Altered scapular kinematics are typical in MDI [r12]. A non-systematic review of painful shoulders with altered scapular kinematics suggests a scapular and trunk postural-correcting strategy first, then scapulothoracic muscle rehabilitation (especially serratus anterior and lower and middle trapezius), and finally neuromotor techniques to recover upper-limb kinematic patterns [r12]. That guidance was not written for MDI specifically and is expert opinion rather than trial evidence.

physio.name: Education, load management and kinetic-chain work
physio.description: Explain laxity versus instability, why muscle control is the target, and how to avoid repeated end-range loading while building capacity. Address trunk and hip control in athletes. A suggested expectation is that an adequate trial of the program is 3–6 months (clinical convention).

physio.name: Post-operative rehabilitation after capsular shift or plication
physio.description: A systematic review of 9 articles found a lack of evidence to indicate the optimal rehabilitation protocol after MDI surgery [r8]. Follow the surgeon's protocol, then progress by criteria.

physio.name: End-range stretching or mobilisation into the direction of laxity
physio.description: Stretching or mobilising an already lax capsule is not logical and may increase symptoms; use targeted mobility work only for coexisting stiffness (for example thoracic spine).

education: Your shoulder has more movement than usual, and it is the muscle control, not just the joint, that keeps it steady. Exercise to improve that control is the first treatment.
The evidence for exercise is limited but encouraging: in the best trial, a specific program improved scores more than a general strengthening program [r5].

Surgery is an option if a full, supervised program fails, but outcomes are not as good as for a shoulder that came out after a single injury, and the best rehabilitation after surgery is not established [r3,r8].
Avoid repeatedly pushing the shoulder to the end of its range, and keep up a long-term maintenance program.
Tell your clinician if you have a fall, a locked shoulder, new numbness or weakness, or your symptoms change.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and aims to build scapular and rotator cuff motor control, then strength and function, while avoiding repeated end-range loading. Trials used 12 weekly physiotherapy sessions with a home program and measured outcomes up to 24 weeks [r5], and a 6-month home-based program in hypermobile patients [r11]. A suggested order is a postural and scapular-correcting strategy, then scapulothoracic muscle rehabilitation, then neuromotor techniques [r12]. Dosages below are typical clinical conventions, criteria override time, and after surgery the surgeon's protocol applies [r8].

stages.name: Education, posture and scapular control
goals: Explain the diagnosis and the plan
Correct posture and scapular position at rest and in mid-range
Activate serratus anterior, lower trapezius and rotator cuff without pain
precautions: Avoid end-range positions and heavy overhead loading
Do not stretch the lax shoulder into end range
After surgery, follow the surgeon's sling and range restrictions

exercises.name: Scapular setting in sitting or standing
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades gently back and down without shrugging

exercises.name: Isometric external and internal rotation at the side
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at 20–30% effort, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Elbow bent, arm at the side, press gently into the wall

exercises.name: Supported elevation in the scapular plane to about 90°
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blade moving smoothly with the arm

exercises.name: Serratus anterior activation (wall slide or punch)
exercises.cues: Let the shoulder blade wrap around the ribs; avoid winging

progressionCriteria: Resting pain 3/10 or less and fewer episodes of slipping
Able to hold the scapula set during gentle arm movement
Understands the plan and performs the home program correctly

stages.name: Motor control and endurance in the working range
goals: Improve scapular upward rotation with elevation
Start closed-chain loading with good control
precautions: Stay below the range where the shoulder slips
Stop if apprehension or a sense of subluxation appears
Low load and high repetitions to build control, not maximal effort

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 15 with a light dumbbell, 3–4 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked to the ribs, rotate slowly

exercises.name: Band row
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down

exercises.name: Scaption raise to 90°
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 with a light dumbbell, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Thumb up, lift in the scapular plane; keep the shoulder blade moving

exercises.name: Quadruped weight shifts and bird-dog
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blades set as the load moves through the arm

exercises.name: Rhythmic stabilisation at low elevation (ball on wall)
exercises.cues: Small, fast co-contractions; stay below the slipping range

progressionCriteria: Normal scapulohumeral rhythm to at least 90° elevation
Cuff endurance improving and no slipping in daily activities
WOSI or MISS improving compared with baseline

stages.name: Strength and functional loading
goals: Build strength to near the other side
Introduce overhead and sport-specific positions gradually
Train kinetic-chain support from trunk and hips
precautions: Progress overhead loading only with good scapular control
Avoid heavy loading at end range

progressionCriteria: Completes sport-specific training without slipping or pain
Strength and control meet agreed criteria

criteria: No episodes of slipping or apprehension in sport-specific and overhead positions
Pain-free, full functional range of motion with good scapular rhythm
External and internal rotation strength about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
Good scapular control and endurance, including push-up plus and overhead press
Kinetic-chain function: single-leg balance, trunk rotation and hip control
Completes graded sport-specific loading without symptoms for 24 hours afterward
Psychologically ready, with a maintenance program in place
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation, internal rotation and scaption compared with the other side
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
Seated single-arm shot-put or medicine-ball throw
WOSI and MISS at the end of rehabilitation [r5]

prognosis: Prognosis depends on the type. In an older series of 140 shoulders, 80% of 66 shoulders with atraumatic subluxation had a good or excellent result with a specific muscle-strengthening exercise program, compared with 16% of 74 shoulders with traumatic subluxation [r6]. In a systematic review of 24 articles (861 shoulders, median follow-up 4.2 years), 21% (52 of 253) of those treated with physiotherapy needed surgery; redislocation occurred in 10% (61 of 608) of shoulders overall after surgery, 7.5% after open capsular shift, 7.8% after arthroscopic plication, 24.5% after thermal shrinkage and 22% after laser-assisted capsulorrhaphy [r7]. Outcomes remain inferior to those of traumatic unidirectional instability [r3]. The randomised comparison of two rehabilitation programs showed gains at 24 weeks [r5], but the longer-term course of rehabilitation-treated MDI, and of MDI in hypermobile patients, was not established in the sources reviewed [r1].
prevention: No MDI-specific prevention trial was identified; the following are clinical conventions
Maintain scapular and rotator cuff control and trunk strength, especially in swimmers, gymnasts and overhead athletes
Avoid repeated end-range loading and deliberate stretching of already lax shoulders
Treat early symptoms with a supervised program before they spread to several directions [r3]
Continue a long-term maintenance program after rehabilitation
clinicalPearls: Laxity is a finding, instability is symptoms: do not treat a high Beighton score or a sulcus alone [r3,r10].

The most convincing trial compared two exercise programs: a specific motor-control program beat a general strengthening program at 12 and 24 weeks, but there is still no randomised trial of exercise versus no treatment [r5,r1].
In hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos or spectrum disorder, home-based programs improved WOSI by 240 to 325 points but kinesiophobia did not change, so consider supervision and psychological support [r11].
Sulcus sign and load-and-shift have only moderate reliability and unproven validity: record the direction and the reproduction of symptoms, and re-test with the same method [r13].
Expect different diagnoses from different clinicians: surgeons weight examination, physiotherapists weight history, so agree explicit criteria before referral [r14].
Avoid thermal or laser shrinkage, and counsel that surgical outcomes remain inferior to traumatic unidirectional instability [r7,r3].

forces.label: Head slips down with little force

captions.text: A young athlete with a lax shoulder stands with the arm relaxed.
Reaching overhead, the lax capsule lets the head drift downward.
In the cocked position the head also slides forward.
Poor muscle control cannot centre the head, so it slips in more than one direction.
There is no single injury: it is repeated slipping with little force.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.
The capsule normally limits how far the head can move in the socket.
In MDI the capsule is lax, so a downward pull opens a gap under the head.
The head slips down with little force.
It can also slip forward and backward, because the laxity is in more than one direction.
The shoulder hurts and feels unstable, and the cuff and scapular muscles must centre the head.
Muscle control, not a single tear, is the main thing to retrain.
Schematic of capsular collagen: crimped, aligned type I fibres.
Repeated end-range loading straightens the crimp.
Repeated overload stretches the fibres, so laxity slowly increases.
If surgery is needed, plication is followed by new collagen that tightens the capsule.
Remodelling aligns the fibres, but dynamic muscle control remains essential.
